problems.unit: Algebraic field extensions and minimal polynomials
problems.title: A basis for $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$
problems.objective: Compute a simple quadratic extension and justify uniqueness of its standard coordinates.
problems.statement: Prove that every element of $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$ has a unique expression $a+b\sqrt2$ with $a,b\in\mathbb Q$. Deduce the degree and give a $\mathbb Q$-basis.
permittedResults: The polynomial $x^2-2$ is irreducible over $\mathbb Q$.
For algebraic $\alpha$, powers below the degree of its minimal polynomial span $F(\alpha)$.
problems.strategy: Reduce rational functions modulo the minimal polynomial and use irrationality of $\sqrt2$ for uniqueness.
hints: The relation $(\sqrt2)^2=2$ reduces every polynomial to degree below $2$.
Because $x^2-2$ is irreducible, $\mathbb Q[\sqrt2]$ is already a field and equals $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$.
If $a+b\sqrt2=0$ and $b\ne0$, then $\sqrt2=-a/b\in\mathbb Q$, a contradiction.

If two expressions agree, their difference gives $a+b\sqrt2=0$; irrationality forces $b=0$ and then $a=0$. Thus $\{1,\sqrt2\}$ is a basis and the degree is $2$.

problems.objective: Prove transitivity and compute both invariants through a biquadratic tower.
problems.statement: For a finite tower $F\subseteq E\subseteq K$, prove $\operatorname{Tr}_{K/F}=\operatorname{Tr}_{E/F}\circ\operatorname{Tr}_{K/E}$ and $N_{K/F}=N_{E/F}\circ N_{K/E}$. Then take $F=\mathbb Q$, $E=\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$, $K=E(\sqrt3)$ and compute the trace and norm of $1+\sqrt2$ from $K$ to $\mathbb Q$.
permittedResults: Trace and norm are respectively the trace and determinant of multiplication maps.
Determinants and traces behave compatibly with restriction of scalars.
problems.strategy: Use block multiplication matrices for transitivity, then treat the element as a scalar over the middle field.
hints: Writing an $E$-basis of $K$ and an $F$-basis of $E$ produces the block matrix identities.
Because $1+\sqrt2\in E$ and $[K:E]=2$, its $K/E$ trace is $2(1+\sqrt2)$ and its norm is $(1+\sqrt2)^2$.
Now $\operatorname{Tr}_{E/\mathbb Q}(2+2\sqrt2)=4$ and $N_{E/\mathbb Q}((1+\sqrt2)^2)=(-1)^2=1$.
problems.solution: Choose compatible product bases for the tower. The block matrix of multiplication shows that taking the large trace is the same as first taking the $K/E$ trace and then the $E/F$ trace; the corresponding determinant identity gives norm transitivity. In the example, an element of $E$ acts as a scalar on the two-dimensional $E$-space $K$, so its relative trace and norm are $2a$ and $a^2$. For $a=1+\sqrt2$, the final trace is $4$, while $N_{E/\mathbb Q}(a)=(1+\sqrt2)(1-\sqrt2)=-1$, so the final norm is $(-1)^2=1$.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the decisive field-theoretic object or calculation correctly: Writing an $E$-basis of $K$ and an $F$-basis of $E$ produces the block matrix identities.
Justifies the central inference without dropping a degree or separability hypothesis: Because $1+\sqrt2\in E$ and $[K:E]=2$, its $K/E$ trace is $2(1+\sqrt2)$ and its norm is $(1+\sqrt2)^2$.
Reaches and explains the requested conclusion: Now $\operatorname{Tr}_{E/\mathbb Q}(2+2\sqrt2)=4$ and $N_{E/\mathbb Q}((1+\sqrt2)^2)=(-1)^2=1$.

problems.unit: Algebraic field extensions and minimal polynomials
problems.title: The full primitive element theorem
problems.objective: Prove that every finite separable extension is simple, including finite and infinite base fields.
problems.statement: Prove the primitive element theorem: if $E/F$ is finite and separable, then $E=F(\theta)$ for some $\theta\in E$. Treat finite and infinite base fields separately.
permittedResults: Every finite extension of a finite field is generated by one element of its cyclic multiplicative group.
Over an infinite field, finitely many bad linear-combination parameters can be avoided.
problems.strategy: Use a multiplicative generator over finite fields and the embedding-separation parameter argument over infinite fields.
hints: If $F$ is finite, then $E$ is finite and $E^\times$ is cyclic; a generator of $E^\times$ generates $E$ as a field.
If $F$ is infinite, reduce inductively to $E=F(\alpha,\beta)$.
Choose $c\in F$ so distinct embeddings take distinct values on $\alpha+c\beta$; then its number of conjugates is $[E:F]$.
problems.solution: When $F$ is finite, so is $E$. Choose a generator $\theta$ of the cyclic group $E^\times$. The field $F(\theta)$ contains every nonzero element of $E$ and also zero, hence equals $E$. Now assume $F$ infinite. A finite separable extension has a finite separable generating set, so induction reduces to $E=F(\alpha,\beta)$. Among the finitely many embeddings, each distinct pair excludes at most one scalar $c$ for which their values on $\alpha+c\beta$ coincide. Choose $c$ outside all bad values. Then $\theta=\alpha+c\beta$ has $[E:F]$ distinct conjugates, so $[F(\theta):F]=[E:F]$ and $F(\theta)=E$.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the decisive field-theoretic object or calculation correctly: If $F$ is finite, then $E$ is finite and $E^\times$ is cyclic; a generator of $E^\times$ generates $E$ as a field.
Justifies the central inference without dropping a degree or separability hypothesis: If $F$ is infinite, reduce inductively to $E=F(\alpha,\beta)$.
Reaches and explains the requested conclusion: Choose $c\in F$ so distinct embeddings take distinct values on $\alpha+c\beta$; then its number of conjugates is $[E:F]$.

commonErrors.consequence: An infinite field's multiplicative group need not be cyclic, so the proof must branch by the size of the base field.

problems.unit: Algebraic field extensions and minimal polynomials
problems.title: The minimal polynomial of $2\cos(2\pi/11)$
problems.objective: Combine cyclotomic symmetry, a recurrence, and the tower law to compute a real cyclotomic minimal polynomial.
problems.statement: Let $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/11}$ and $u=\zeta+\zeta^{-1}=2\cos(2\pi/11)$. Using $s_k=\zeta^k+\zeta^{-k}$, prove that the minimal polynomial of $u$ over $\mathbb Q$ is $x^5+x^4-4x^3-3x^2+3x+1$. Deduce that $\mathbb Q(u)$ is the degree-five real subfield of $\mathbb Q(\zeta)$ and give a power basis.
permittedResults: $[\mathbb Q(\zeta):\mathbb Q]=\varphi(11)=10$.
The element $\zeta$ has minimal polynomial $x^2-ux+1$ over $\mathbb Q(u)$.
Tower law.
problems.strategy: Generate the symmetric powers by a second-order recurrence, use the cyclotomic sum for an annihilating polynomial, and certify minimality by a degree computation.
hints: The identity $(\zeta+\zeta^{-1})(\zeta^k+\zeta^{-k})=s_{k+1}+s_{k-1}$ gives $s_{k+1}=us_k-s_{k-1}$ with $s_0=2$ and $s_1=u$.
Compute through $s_5$, then use $1+s_1+s_2+s_3+s_4+s_5=0$, obtained by pairing terms in $1+\zeta+\cdots+\zeta^{10}=0$.
Because $[\mathbb Q(\zeta):\mathbb Q(u)]=2$, the tower law gives $[\mathbb Q(u):\mathbb Q]=5$; a monic degree-five annihilator is therefore minimal.
problems.solution: The product identity gives the recurrence $s_{k+1}=us_k-s_{k-1}$. Starting from $s_0=2$ and $s_1=u$, it yields $s_2=u^2-2$, $s_3=u^3-3u$, $s_4=u^4-4u^2+2$, and $s_5=u^5-5u^3+5u$. Pairing inverse powers in the cyclotomic relation $1+\zeta+\cdots+\zeta^{10}=0$ gives $1+s_1+s_2+s_3+s_4+s_5=0$. Substitution and collection of terms produce $u^5+u^4-4u^3-3u^2+3u+1=0$. The permitted quadratic relation shows $[\mathbb Q(\zeta):\mathbb Q(u)]=2$, while the cyclotomic degree is $10$; hence the tower law gives $[\mathbb Q(u):\mathbb Q]=5$. The displayed monic degree-five annihilator is therefore the minimal polynomial. Every element of $\mathbb Q(\zeta)$ has the form $a+b\zeta$ with $a,b\in\mathbb Q(u)$. If it is real, conjugation gives $a+b\zeta=a+b\zeta^{-1}$, so $b=0$ because $\zeta\ne\zeta^{-1}$. Thus $\mathbb Q(u)$ is exactly the real subfield, with power basis $1,u,u^2,u^3,u^4$.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the decisive field-theoretic object or calculation correctly: The identity $(\zeta+\zeta^{-1})(\zeta^k+\zeta^{-k})=s_{k+1}+s_{k-1}$ gives $s_{k+1}=us_k-s_{k-1}$ with $s_0=2$ and $s_1=u$.

Justifies the central inference without dropping a degree or separability hypothesis: Compute through $s_5$, then use $1+s_1+s_2+s_3+s_4+s_5=0$, obtained by pairing terms in $1+\zeta+\cdots+\zeta^{10}=0$.
Reaches and explains the requested conclusion: Because $[\mathbb Q(\zeta):\mathbb Q(u)]=2$, the tower law gives $[\mathbb Q(u):\mathbb Q]=5$; a monic degree-five annihilator is therefore minimal.

problems.title: Pure inseparability creates nilpotents after tensoring
problems.objective: Compute a self-base-change of a purely inseparable field and exhibit its nilpotent structure.
problems.statement: Let $F$ have characteristic $p>0$, let $a\in F$ not be a $p$th power, and set $K=F(u)$ with $u^p=a$. Prove $K\otimes_F K\cong K[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^p)$ and identify a nonzero nilpotent. Contrast this with the separable quadratic computation $L\otimes_F L\cong L\times L$.
permittedResults: $K\cong F[x]/(x^p-a)$ and base change gives $K\otimes_FK\cong K[x]/(x^p-a)$.
In characteristic $p$, $x^p-u^p=(x-u)^p$.
problems.strategy: Base-change the defining equation and translate the repeated root to a nilpotent variable.
hints: Over $K$, the polynomial becomes $x^p-u^p=(x-u)^p$.
Set $\varepsilon=x-u$; then the quotient relation is exactly $\varepsilon^p=0$.
The class of $\varepsilon$ is nonzero because its degree is below $p$, while separable base change has distinct factors and a reduced product.
problems.solution: Using $K\cong F[x]/(x^p-a)$, base change gives $K\otimes_FK\cong K[x]/(x^p-a)$. Since $a=u^p$ and the characteristic is $p$, the modulus is $(x-u)^p$. Translating by $\varepsilon=x-u$ identifies the quotient with $K[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^p)$. The class of $\varepsilon$ is nonzero but its $p$th power is zero, so the tensor product is nonreduced. For a separable quadratic, the two distinct linear factors are comaximal and CRT gives a reduced product $L\times L$ instead.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the decisive field-theoretic object or calculation correctly: Over $K$, the polynomial becomes $x^p-u^p=(x-u)^p$.
Justifies the central inference without dropping a degree or separability hypothesis: Set $\varepsilon=x-u$; then the quotient relation is exactly $\varepsilon^p=0$.
Reaches and explains the requested conclusion: The class of $\varepsilon$ is nonzero because its degree is below $p$, while separable base change has distinct factors and a reduced product.

commonErrors.consequence: The repeated factor created by purely inseparable base change produces nilpotents and destroys field structure.

problems.title: Trace, norm, and discriminant in $\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]{2})$
problems.objective: Compute arithmetic invariants of a cubic extension from all three embeddings.
problems.statement: Let $K=\mathbb Q(\alpha)$ with $\alpha^3=2$. Compute the traces and norms of $\alpha$ and $1+\alpha$, and compute the discriminant of the power basis $1,\alpha,\alpha^2$.
permittedResults: For a monic minimal polynomial, the norm of $c-\alpha$ is its value at $c$.
The discriminant of $x^3+ax+b$ is $-4a^3-27b^2$.
problems.strategy: Use the conjugates $\alpha,\omega\alpha,\omega^2\alpha$ and the discriminant of $x^3-2$.
hints: The sum of the three conjugates of $\alpha$ is $0$ and their product is $2$.
For $1+\alpha$, trace adds $3$, while $N(1+\alpha)=-m_\alpha(-1)=3$.
The power-basis discriminant equals the polynomial discriminant of $x^3-2$, namely $-108$.
problems.solution: The conjugates are $\alpha,\omega\alpha,\omega^2\alpha$. Their sum is zero and product is $\alpha^3\omega^3=2$, so $\operatorname{Tr}(\alpha)=0$ and $N(\alpha)=2$. Finally the power-basis discriminant is the discriminant of $x^3-2$, which is $-27(-2)^2=-108$.

Justifies the central inference without dropping a degree or separability hypothesis: For $1+\alpha$, trace adds $3$, while $N(1+\alpha)=-m_\alpha(-1)=3$.

problems.unit: Algebraic field extensions and minimal polynomials
problems.title: A finite-field degree-six capstone
problems.objective: Synthesize subfields, exact-degree counts, irreducible counts, trace, and norm in one finite field.
problems.statement: Let $E=\mathbb F_{q^6}$ over $F=\mathbb F_q$. List all subfields, count the elements of exact degree $6$ over $F$, deduce the number of monic irreducible sextics over $F$, and state the trace and norm formulas for $a\in E$.
permittedResults: Finite-field subfield criterion.
Inclusion-exclusion on the divisor lattice.
Frobenius formulas for trace and norm.
problems.strategy: Use divisors of six for the lattice, Möbius inversion for exact degree, and Frobenius conjugates for the invariants.
hints: The subfields have sizes $q,q^2,q^3,q^6$.
Exact degree six contributes $q^6-q^3-q^2+q$ elements; divide by six for monic irreducibles.
Trace is $\sum_{j=0}^{5}a^{q^j}$ and norm is $a^{1+q+\cdots+q^5}=a^{(q^6-1)/(q-1)}$.

Elements of proper degree lie in the degree-two or degree-three subfields, whose intersection is the degree-one field. Inclusion-exclusion therefore gives $q^6-q^3-q^2+q$ elements of exact degree six. Each irreducible sextic contributes six conjugate roots, so their number is $(q^6-q^3-q^2+q)/6$. Finally $\operatorname{Tr}(a)=\sum_{j=0}^{5}a^{q^j}$ and $N(a)=a^{(q^6-1)/(q-1)}$.

problems.unit: Algebraic field extensions and minimal polynomials
problems.title: A compositum and tensor-product comparison
problems.objective: Prove a tensor product is a field by comparing its dimension with a coprime-degree compositum.
problems.statement: Let $L=\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]{2})$ and $M=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$. Prove that the natural map $L\otimes_{\mathbb Q}M\to LM$ is an isomorphism, compute the degree, and explain why $LM$ is the splitting field of $x^3-2$.
permittedResults: Coprime-degree compositum theorem.
A surjective linear map between finite-dimensional spaces of equal dimension is an isomorphism.
problems.strategy: Use degrees three and two to get a six-dimensional compositum, then compare dimensions and identify the cube root of unity.
hints: The two extension degrees are $3$ and $2$, hence their intersection is $\mathbb Q$ and $[LM:\mathbb Q]=6$.
The multiplication map from the tensor product is surjective and both source and target have dimension six.
The field $M$ contains $\omega=(-1+\sqrt{-3})/2$, so $LM$ contains all three roots of $x^3-2$.
problems.solution: Eisenstein gives $[L:\mathbb Q]=3$, while $M$ is quadratic. Coprimality yields trivial intersection and compositum degree six. The multiplication map $L\otimes_{\mathbb Q}M\to LM$ is surjective because pure products generate the compositum; its source has dimension $3\cdot2=6$, equal to the target dimension, so it is injective as well. Finally $M$ contains a primitive cube root $\omega=(-1+\sqrt{-3})/2$, and $LM$ contains $\alpha,\omega\alpha,\omega^2\alpha$, all roots of $x^3-2$.
rubricCriteria: Sets up the decisive field-theoretic object or calculation correctly: The two extension degrees are $3$ and $2$, hence their intersection is $\mathbb Q$ and $[LM:\mathbb Q]=6$.
Justifies the central inference without dropping a degree or separability hypothesis: The multiplication map from the tensor product is surjective and both source and target have dimension six.
Reaches and explains the requested conclusion: The field $M$ contains $\omega=(-1+\sqrt{-3})/2$, so $LM$ contains all three roots of $x^3-2$.

problems.title: Every intermediate field of a biquadratic extension
problems.objective: Determine a complete intermediate-field lattice and prove that no fields are missing.
problems.statement: Let $K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$. Prove that its complete list of intermediate fields is $\mathbb Q$, $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$, $\mathbb Q(\sqrt3)$, $\mathbb Q(\sqrt6)$, and $K$.

The four independent sign changes are all $\mathbb Q$-automorphisms of $K$.
The orbit of an element under these automorphisms consists of roots of its minimal polynomial.

hints: Tower degrees force every proper nontrivial intermediate field to have degree $2$.
If $\theta$ generates such a field, its four sign-change images include at most two distinct roots of its quadratic minimal polynomial, so some nonidentity sign change fixes $\theta$.

problems.unit: Algebraic field extensions and minimal polynomials
problems.title: An algebraic tower over a rational function field
problems.objective: Synthesize algebraic independence, tower degree, a product basis, and transcendence degree.
problems.statement: Let $s,t$ be algebraically independent over $\mathbb Q$, set $F=\mathbb Q(s,t)$, and in an algebraic closure choose $u,v$ with $u^2=s$ and $v^3=t$. For $K=F(u,v)$, prove $[K:F]=6$, give an $F$-basis, and prove $\operatorname{trdeg}_{\mathbb Q}K=2$ with transcendence basis $\{s,t\}$.
permittedResults: Eisenstein's criterion over a UFD and its fraction field.
Tower law.
Finite algebraic extensions preserve transcendence degree.
problems.strategy: Use the prime variables $s$ and $t$ in two Eisenstein arguments, multiply the power bases, then pass transcendence degree through the finite algebraic extension.
hints: Over $\mathbb Q(s,t)$, $x^2-s$ is irreducible by the $s$-adic valuation or Eisenstein in $\mathbb Q[s,t]$.
After adjoining $u$, the variable $t$ remains transcendental over $\mathbb Q(s,u)$, so $x^3-t$ is Eisenstein at $t$ and contributes degree $3$.
The six products $u^iv^j$ for $0\le i<2$, $0\le j<3$ form a basis; since $K/F$ is algebraic, $s,t$ remain a transcendence basis.
problems.solution: The polynomial $x^2-s$ is Eisenstein at the prime $s$ in $\mathbb Q[s,t]$, so $[F(u):F]=2$. In $F(u)=\mathbb Q(s,u)(t)$, the element $t$ is still an indeterminate, and $x^3-t$ is Eisenstein at $t$ over the UFD $\mathbb Q(s,u)[t]$. Hence $[K:F(u)]=3$ and the tower degree is $6$. Multiplying the power bases gives $1,v,v^2,u,uv,uv^2$. Finally $K/F$ is finite algebraic, while $F=\mathbb Q(s,t)$ has transcendence degree two. Algebraic extension preserves transcendence degree, so $\{s,t\}$ is a transcendence basis of $K/\mathbb Q$.

problems.objective: verify degree, normality, separability, and automorphisms in a quadratic example
problems.statement: Let $K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)$. Find a $\mathbb Q$-basis of $K$, determine the minimal polynomial of $\sqrt2$, list all $\mathbb Q$-automorphisms of $K$, and prove that $K/\mathbb Q$ is Galois.
permittedResults: A finite extension is Galois exactly when it is normal and separable
problems.strategy: Use irreducibility of $x^2-2$, observe that both roots lie in the generated field, and determine an automorphism by the image of the generator.
hints: The polynomial $x^2-2$ is irreducible over $\mathbb Q$, so $(1,\sqrt2)$ is a basis.
Any automorphism sends $\sqrt2$ to another root, namely $\sqrt2$ or $-\sqrt2$.
The polynomial splits in $K$ and has distinct roots, giving normality and separability.

Since $x^2-2=(x-\sqrt2)(x+\sqrt2)$ splits in $K$ and has no repeated root, the extension is normal and separable, hence Galois, with group $C_2$.
